-111.75700,32.93500.state: Eloy, Arizona — Biorubber Process Research Center
-111.75700,32.93500.desc: Develops guayule, a desert shrub, as a domestic rubber source, using genomic selection and editing to raise latex yield. Nearly all natural rubber comes from one tropical species descended from a narrow collection made in the 1870s, grown mostly in one region — so a second source in a different climate is a hedge against a single disease outbreak taking the supply for tyres and surgical gloves at once.

4.38100,50.84350.name: EU Group of Chief Scientific Advisors
4.38100,50.84350.desc: Advises the European Commission before a proposal is written. Its 2018 opinion on new genomic techniques, published after the Court held that editing falls under the GMO directive, is the document the Commission's subsequent legislative proposal rests on. Reading it explains where that proposal came from better than the proposal does.

176.28000,-38.16000.name: Scion — New Zealand Forest Research Institute
176.28000,-38.16000.desc: The Crown research institute running what its own page calls the only plant GM field trial currently operating in New Zealand, on a four-hectare containment site approved in 2010 and continuing to 2035. It has been field-testing engineered pine since around 1996. The controls are the most specific on this map: trees must be felled at eight years or as soon as they begin to develop reproductive structures, inspections must find male catkins or female cones soon after they form, and those must be removed within 24 hours and destroyed. Its published annual reports record each transfer from glasshouse to field by date and permit number, and the ministry audits. Whatever one concludes about the research, this is the clearest documented example of what containment actually consists of — people walking a plot looking for cones — and it is worth setting against the Chinese poplar entry where nobody could say how much had been planted.
